Vancouver

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF
BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:                          )

)

LYNDA JOYCE TAYLOR      )
REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

)

PLAINTIFF     )

)

OF THE HONOURABLE

AND:                              )

)

CLIVE TAYLOR       )

MR. JUSTICE FRASER

)

DEFENDANT     )

)

AND:                              )

)

CAMPBELL, SAUNDERS LTD.      )

)

TRUSTEE IN BANKRUPTCY     )

OF CLIVE TAYLOR     )

)

M. Edward Mortimer, Q.C.             Counsel
for the Plaintiff

and Jeffrey Rose

Karen F. Nordlinger, Q.C.            Counsel
for the Defendant

and Dagmar Dlab

John F. Grieve           Counsel for
the Trustee in Bankruptcy

Place of Hearing:                              Vancouver,
B.C.

1
What the formerly-married Mr. and
Mrs. Taylor seek in this star-crossed litigation is a determination which of
their assets are family assets within the meaning of the
Family Relations
Act
[1]
and a division of those
assets.  The plaintiff, Lynda Joyce Taylor, also seeks an order for permanent
maintenance for herself, pursuant to the
Divorce Act
,
1985
[2]
.

2
I say "star-crossed"
because, in addition to the complexity of the case itself (at least, as first
presented), a succession of unusual and unanticipated events, including what is
in this Court a rarity
──
the apparent mishandling and loss of documents
──
has conspired to delay its
disposition.  (The documents were ultimately found).  The first Court day was
26th November 1990.  The last day was 8th June 1995.  The evidence tendered
since 1991 has been in affidavit form.  Written submissions were filed in 1991,
1992, 1994 and 1995.  Even after this judgment is delivered, there is the
prospect that the case will come back again for consequential relief.

3
The most important delaying factor
was the bankruptcy of Mr. Taylor.  I heard 10 days of evidence in 1990 and 1991
and the case was then adjourned for the delivery of written submissions.  Mr.
Mortimer, on behalf of Mrs. Taylor, delivered submissions on 22nd August 1991.
On 27th September 1991, Mr. Taylor assigned himself into bankruptcy.  I added
the trustee in bankruptcy, Campbell, Saunders Ltd., as a party.  Submissions
from counsel on behalf of the Trustee were filed in June 1992 and June 1994.
Distribution of the bankruptcy estate of Mr. Taylor awaits these reasons.  Mr.
Taylor gave evidence that he was discharged from bankruptcy on 21st December
1992 but the attempt to identify assets of the bankrupt estate went on well
after that.

4
Mr. Mortimer and Ms. Nordlinger are
among the leaders of the British Columbia Bar.  I wish to record that none of
the lapse of time since the bankruptcy of Mr. Taylor seems to me the fault of
either of them.  Nor have I been given any reason to believe that there was
undue delay in the bankruptcy or on the part of Mr. Grieve, counsel for the
trustee.  I was informed by counsel by a letter of 13th September 1995 that the
case was ready for disposition.

THE HISTORY OF THE MARRIAGE

5
Lynda Joyce Taylor was born on 23rd
July 1946.  Clive Taylor was born on 14th April 1943.  When they began to live
together in March, 1980, then, she was 33 years old and he was 36.  They
married on 11th March 1983.

6
It was a second marriage for both.
Mr. Taylor had children from his first marriage.  His daughter Candice lived
with Mr. and Mrs. Taylor during the relationship and marriage.  There is
dispute about Mrs. Taylor's involvement with Candice.  I find that Candice
lived with Mr. and Mrs. Taylor for significant periods of time and was with
them from time to time throughout.  When Candice was there, Mrs. Taylor worked
at creating a harmonious family atmosphere and in being a good stepmother.  She
was genuinely fond of Candice
──
the "daughter I never had" was how she put it.   To the
extent that Candice's testimony did not reflect this, my conclusion is that it
was influenced by loyalty to her father, at a time when she could see that her
father had nothing good to say about Mrs. Taylor.  Candice's letter to Mrs.
Taylor of 30th April 1989 (Exhibit 48) had a very different tone, affectionate
and anxious to re-connect.

7
The parties separated in February
1989 and a declaration under Section 44 of the
Family Relations Act

that there was no prospect of reconciliation was made by this Court on 16th
March 1989.  The parties were divorced by an Order made by me on 25th March
1993.  When they separated, Mrs. Taylor was 42 and Mr. Taylor was 45.

8
Mrs. Taylor had been employed and
self-employed before she and Mr. Taylor began to live together.  I find on the
evidence that she demonstrated some considerable ability in the various jobs
that she had.  None of them, however, was one holding the prospect of long-term
or permanent employment.  Her situation was uncertain.

9
When they met, Mr. Taylor was a
successful life insurance salesman.  It was during the marriage that he had his
best years.  He represented the Transamerica Life Insurance Company.  His gross
commission income in 1985 was $590,976.53.  In 1986, it was $669,005.76.  In
1987, it was $456,521.  In 1988, it was $526,757.

10
Part of the income stream during
these years consisted of commission override from the commissions of other
agents, during a time when Mr. Taylor was acting as a Branch Manager.  He gave
notice that he would cease to be Branch Manager effective 31st December 1988.
This is reflected in the drop in his commission income in 1989, down to
$371,292.  However, it increased again to $430,433 in 1990.

11
The gross commission numbers do not begin
to show the whole picture.  Mr. Taylor made the mistake, as do so many high
income earners, of elaborating his financial situation for income tax reasons.
One acronym will do: MURBs.  The result was disaster.

12
I find that Mr. Taylor was not
interested in the money that Mrs. Taylor might have been able to earn if she
were employed. It would have been a pittance compared to his.  What was more
important to him was to have a partner and, later, wife, who did the work to
stage the activities which defined his lifestyle.  He liked having a vivacious
consort who could fill this role.  This is just what Mrs. Taylor did.  He was
earning big money and they played and entertained accordingly.

13
The perfect metaphor for their roles
in the marriage has to do with their boat, the "Candolyn".  She was
moored at Secret Cove, up the coast from Vancouver.  Between April and October,
Mr. and Mrs. Taylor went to Secret Cove almost every weekend.  To travel
between Vancouver and Secret Cove by car involves a ferry trip; often,
especially on Fridays and Sundays, there are lineups for the ferry, and
delays.  For their weekends on the boat, which sometimes involved entertaining
others, Mrs. Taylor would leave for Secret Cove early on Friday in a car,
loaded with the provisions for the weekend.  She would open up the boat and
prepare as necessary when she got there.  Mr. Taylor would nip up on Friday,
after work, on his motorcycle.  This gave him immediate access to the ferry,
without having to wait in line.  They would enjoy the weekend together, with or
without guests.  He would go back to Vancouver Sunday night on the motorcycle,
again bypassing any lineup.  Mrs. Taylor would clean up, close up and return on
Monday in the car, when the ferry traffic was light.

14
Mr. and Mrs. Taylor disagreed in
their evidence as to the extent of her involvement in business entertainment
for the benefit of Mr. Taylor.  I find that, like many whose income depends on
sales, Mr. Taylor's social life was one of mixed business and pleasure.  What
entertainment there was, she staged.  When he travelled, she travelled, except
for events like the "Million Dollar Club" conventions, to which
spouses were not invited.

15
As sometimes happens, things began to
disintegrate at various points on the matrimonial map at the same time.  As
Mrs. Taylor's medical problems became more serious, Mr. Taylor's commitment to
her was waning, although I do not see a necessary linkage between these two
developments.  By the time of her hospitalization in February 1989, the
marriage was in crisis.  By the time she was discharged, it was effectively
over.  In reciting this, I am not introducing misconduct as a factor in these
reasons; I do find that Mrs. Taylor was committed to the marriage and that its
breakdown was, for her, a dreadful event.  This cannot, it seems to me, be
ignored in assessing the "pull up your socks" stance of Mr. Taylor on
the issue of maintenance.

PERMANENT MAINTENANCE FOR MRS. TAYLOR

16
In 1985, Mrs. Taylor began to
experience chest pains.  After a series of tests, she was diagnosed as having
achalasia of the esophagus, that is, abnormal contraction of the esophagus.  In
March 1988, a procedure known as a balloon dilation was performed on her to
relieve her condition, by expanding the esophagal sphincter.  A second dilation
was performed in April 1988.  Unfortunately, on this second occasion, the
procedure itself ruptured Mrs. Taylor's esophagus, necessitating emergency open
chest surgery.  During recovery, infection developed at the site of the surgery
and a second open chest surgery resulted.  All this kept Mrs. Taylor in the
hospital for something like a month.

17
She underwent rectal surgery in
February 1989, for a condition secondary to the pain medication she was taking.

18
Dr. Albert Ho Yee, Mrs. Taylor's
doctor, reported to Mr. Mortimer in a letter of 11th March 1989 that Mrs.
Taylor's second post-operative period, that is, the period following the
infection-driven surgery, was "very stormy and prolonged".  He said
that the ultimate end result of the surgery had left Mrs. Taylor with constant
pain in the left side of her chest, aggravated by position changes of her body,
deep breathing, coughing and sneezing.

19
Dr. Yee also observed tenderness over
the whole of the left side of Mrs. Taylor's anterior chest wall, which he
diagnosed as "post-operative costochondritis".  In his letter to Mr.
Mortimer of 28th April 1990, Dr. Yee described costochondritis as "an
inflammatory condition secondary to the trauma of her surgery".

20
Dr. Yee regarded the costochondritis
as very debilitating, "in the sense that it restricts her activity, it can
fluctuate in intensity, and responds poorly to treatment".

21
As at 11th March 1989, it was the
opinion of Dr. Yee that Mrs. Taylor was "totally incapacitated" for
employment and would continue to be so for at least the next 12 months.

22
In a letter to Mr. Mortimer of 14th
March 1989, Dr. Yee said that it was not uncommon for post-operative chest wall
pain to persist from anywhere between 2 and 5 years.

23
A little more than a year later, on
28th April 1990, Dr. Yee wrote again to Mr. Mortimer.  Her condition he
described then as "intermittent leftsided chest wall pain, as a result of
costochondritis".  He gave it as his opinion that Mrs. Taylor was capable
of some form of employment, provided that it did not involve frequent movement
such as bending over, reaching overhead or outwards, or lifting.

24
Later in 1990, Mrs. Taylor was
referred by her psychiatrist, Dr. Stephen Kline, to Dr. May C. Ong-Lam, a specialist
in the diagnosis and management of pain.  Dr. Ong-Lam reported to Dr. Kline
concerning Mrs. Taylor's "ongoing leftsided post-thoracotomy pain".
(Surgical entry into the chest is known as thoracotomy).  It is apparent to me
that Dr. Ong-Lam did not doubt that there was ongoing pain.  She put Mrs.
Taylor on a recovery program.  As at 24th October 1990, the expectation of Dr.
Ong-Lam was that there would be recovery "toward part-time or full-time
employment in the period of up to two years from now".

25
Dr. Ong-Lam testified in 1990 that
Mrs. Taylor's pain was not constant but surfaced unpredictably and its onset
could not be avoided.  This unpredictability, she said, is the most difficult
thing for patients to accept.  Dr. Ong-Lam said that it was very difficult to
predict the duration of the symptoms.  It would be at least a year and up to
two years.  This was in 1990.

26
She described Mrs. Taylor as a
cooperative patient who followed advice.

27
Possibly because Dr. Kline was Mrs.
Taylor's psychiatrist, Dr. Ong-Lam made some personal observations in her
report to him, as follows:

She is going through
difficult separation and currently unemployed.  She became quite emotional when
she speaks of her separation.

This was on 1st August 1990, some 18
months after the separation.

28
A report of a Dr. Kenneth G. Evans of
14th March 1989 was referred to during the trial but never put in evidence,
although, mysteriously, it is attached to Exhibit 5, an unrelated document.

29
Ms. Nordlinger retained Dr. Charles
Robert Rally, a specialist in internal medicine, to examine Mrs. Taylor.  He
did so on 16th November 1990.  Dr. Rally is involved in disability assessment:
he does a great deal of it for insurance companies, the Workers' Compensation
Board and serves (for the Government, I imagine) on appeal panels which hear
disability claims for British Columbia government employees.

30
Dr. Rally stated that an individual
who does well from a thoracotomy "should be completely free of chest pain
three or four months after the surgery".  He seemed reluctant to agree
with Dr. Yee's diagnosis of post-operative costochondritis.  He felt that Mrs.
Taylor should be able to work.  He said, "I have known many individuals
with much more serious medical problems in what would appear to be in much more
intense pain who have been capable of full-time work".  I find Dr. Rally's
evidence to be general and statistical in its form; and of little value when
set against that of the doctors who have treated Mrs. Taylor.

31
Updated medical information about
Mrs. Taylor was put before me, in the form of another report from Dr. Yee.  As
of the date of the report, 15th February 1995, Dr. Yee was still seeing Mrs.
Taylor about "ongoing chest pain" resulting from the thoracic surgery
of 1988.  Evidently, Mrs. Taylor has seen a number of physicians about and
tried a variety of techniques to relieve her pain.  The most recent procedures
have involved cryosurgery, that is, the injection of solutions to desensitize
the intercostal nerves.  Two such procedures were performed in 1991, another in
1993 and another in January 1994.  Another was coming up.  Dr. Yee said that
they offered her "partial and temporary relief for variable intervals of
time".  Dr. Yee said that Mrs. Taylor was "very symptomatic"
from her pain.  He stated: "To summarize, Lynda remains totally disabled
because of her chest pain."

32
He stated that she had undertaken
some limited part-time employment as an instructor in teaching seniors at
dancing but said that she had been able to manage only a few hours of such
activity weekly.

33
He went on to say: "The
prognosis for recovery from her chest pain at this time looks bleak.  I do not
anticipate that she will ever be able to undertake any full-time gainful
employment at anytime in the future."

34
On 10th March 1995, without being
asked to do so, I gave Mr. Taylor an opportunity to generate updated medical
evidence by directing Mrs. Taylor to submit to a further examination for
discovery on the maintenance issue alone and to submit to a medical examination
at the behest of Mr. Taylor by a doctor agreed to by her counsel.  Neither of
these opportunities have been taken up so far by Mr. Taylor.

35
Mrs. Taylor's evidence as to her
medical condition can be summarized by saying that her problems are
debilitating, keep her in chronic pain and prevent her from finding employment.

36
From the point of view of Mr. Taylor,
Mrs. Taylor is making heavy weather of medical conditions and problems from
which she should have recovered long ago.  Mrs. Taylor did agree, in her
testimony of 27th November 1990, that she had gone fishing, had put on some
dinner parties, had attempted to golf and regularly walked the seawall around
Stanley Park.

37
The presentation on behalf of Mr.
Taylor is to the effect that, so long as Mrs. Taylor receives substantial
support from him,  she will be content to lark about, rather than seek to
become economically self-sufficient.

38
Mrs. Taylor began receiving monthly
court-ordered support payments from Mr. Taylor of $2,200 per month on 1st April
1989, within two months of the separation, which were automatically increased
to $3,000 per month on 1st November 1989, after she moved out of the
matrimonial home.  She continues to receive $3,000 per month.

39
This means that, up to the date of
this judgment, Mrs. Taylor has received support payments over almost 7 years
totalling more than $225,000.  This is a lot of money but it needs a context.
It is less than Mr. Taylor's gross income in 1989 alone, which was for him a
bad
──

though not his worst
──
year.  It is just more than 1/3 of his gross income in 1986, his best
year during the relationship.  He is still doing well.  And, of course, the
real cost to him of the support payments is reduced by tax provisions, while
she is taxed on the payments.

40
During the marriage, Mr. Taylor gave
Mrs. Taylor an "allowance" of $2,200, then $2,500, then $3,100 per
month.  This was for groceries, liquor and for her spending money.  (The
increase from $2,500 to $3,100 reflected newly-incurred car lease payments.)
Major household bills
──
rent, hydro, telephone, credit cards
──
were sent to Mr. Taylor's office and
paid from there.  The allowance was routed through his company, Clive Taylor
Agencies Ltd., as a salary to her and claimed by the company as a business
expense for tax purposes.  Mr. Taylor found the money for the income tax payable
by her on the T-4's issued to her.  Since, for tax purposes, Clive Taylor
Agencies Ltd. and Mr. Taylor were one and the same, the cost to him of the
allowance was minimized by this device.  I will have more to say about this
later.

41
In terms of the criteria set out in
sub-sections (5) and (7) of
s.15
of the
Divorce Act
, 1985, my
findings are these:

1.The
parties co-habited from March 1980 to February 1989, a period of 9 years, save
for a brief separation before marriage.

2.The
functions performed by Mrs. Taylor during co-habitation were, by mutual
consent, designed to dovetail with Mr. Taylor's work patterns and to serve
their shared social and recreational tastes.  Mrs. Taylor had no employment or
social activity during the relationship which brought her independent
recognition.

3.Mr.
Taylor reaped an economic advantage from the marriage in the sense that, in
every aspect of his life other than making his sales, Mrs. Taylor covered for
him.  She freed him up to do what he did well.

4.Mr.
Taylor did not suffer any economic disadvantage arising from the breakdown of
the marriage.  His financial problems arose from unfortunate financial
adventures.

5.Mrs.
Taylor reaped some economic advantage from the marriage.  She received
$104,915.18 from Mr. Taylor in October 1989, representing a one-half interest
in the matrimonial home.

6.Other
than that, the marriage brought economic disadvantage to Mrs. Taylor.  She has
a year of post-secondary education and secretarial training.  The employment
she had before she began to live with Mr. Taylor was transient but it gave
clear signs that she had desirable and marketable attributes as someone who
could, if she wished to, take on and discharge important and responsible
duties.  An interruption of 9 years in the world of employment, between the ages
of 33 and 42, is a significant one.  I take
Moge v. Moge
[3]
, as interpreted by Prowse
J.A. for the majority in the decision of our Court of Appeal in
Toth v.
Toth
[4]
, as indicating that a trial
court does not require elaborate evidence in order to determine whether there
has or has not been an economic disadvantage to a spouse.

It
seems to me, as well, that one need not be an expert in some discipline or
other to recognize that 9 years of life in a moneyed world adds to the
difficulty of re-entering the employment market at the bottom.

On
the other hand, I do not think it can be said that Mrs. Taylor, before she
began to live with Mr. Taylor, showed great inclination to the world of
employment.

7.The
economic self-sufficiency of Mr. Taylor is not an issue.  The impact of this
judgment on Mr. Taylor, whatever it might be, can only be marginal to his
financial situation at large.

8.The
economic self-sufficiency of Mrs. Taylor is more problematic.  Even if she were
healthy, it is not clear to me that any amount of maintenance would contribute
to her economic self-sufficiency, as opposed to deflecting her from it.  My
sense is that, for her, employment is an unfulfilling exercise, to be
undertaken from necessity, rather than something having any intangible rewards
or satisfactions of its own.

42
Having gone through the exercise of
examining the individual criteria specified in the subclauses of subsections
(5) and (7) of
s. 15
, which I see as virtually obligatory, I can say that they
are mainly overwhelmed by the medical evidence, which brings into play the more
important and governing words of subsection (5), requiring me to consider the
needs and other circumstances of Mrs. Taylor.

43
On the medical evidence, she is
unemployable.

44
Dr. Yee did not testify at the
trial.  Aside from a sort of generalized stance on the part of Mr. Taylor that
he is not objective, that he is too sympathetic to Mrs. Taylor, a familiar
allegation in litigation where a family doctor expresses a view supporting the
contention of a patient, there is nothing to suggest that his diagnosis is
incorrect.

45
So far as the means, needs and other
circumstances of Mr. Taylor are concerned, the water remains murky.  His
financial situation might be helped by termination or reduction of his
maintenance obligations to Mrs. Taylor but it is difficult to see those
payments as a significant factor in his situation.  Since the divorce, he has
remarried and now has an infant child.  He lives in La Jolla, California, where
he is carrying on his work as a life insurance salesman for Transamerica.  He
bought a home there on Ladybird Lane for U.S. $533,000.00.  His RSP has
appreciated since the separation from $210,000 to $415,000.  His financial relationship
to Transamerica, which I understand has always remained outside the orbit of
the bankruptcy, continues to be tangled.  Some of his commission income is
being employed to reduce money which Transamerica says he still owes to it.

46
I do think that Mr. Taylor has a
significant ability to shape his financial relationships with Transamerica.  He
is too valuable a salesman for them to lose.  To the extent that Transamerica
has moved against Mr. Taylor in apparently harsh ways, these moves have been
consistent with Mr. Taylor's interests in this litigation.

47
It is true that Mrs. Taylor herself
is no slouch in the spending department.  She went on a spree immediately after
the separation, racking up some $10,000.00 in credit card bills.  She justified
the purchase of new furs at that time on the basis that her existing fur coats
"were in rags".  In her testimony, she characterized her budget for
cosmetics of $250.00 per month as "rock bottom".  But the concern is
her present needs.

48
I can find no basis at this time on
which to reduce the present level of maintenance.  It will therefore continue
at $3,000 per month.

49
However, the division of assets
between the parties may affect Mrs. Taylor's continuing need for maintenance;
and I think it just to permit further examination of her health and her
willingness to seek employment.  My order of 10th March 1995 will therefore
remain in place and either party may apply to revisit amount of maintenance of
being paid.

THE ASSETS

- PRELIMINARY CONSIDERATIONS

50
In this portion of the judgment, I
will embark upon the usual, mechanical analysis, in which the assets are listed,
their character considered and their division ordered.  Before doing that,
however, a few comments may help to clarify my analyses.

51
The crucial evidence in the trial was
that of Mr. and Mrs. Taylor and of Joyce Mair, Mrs. Taylor's mother.  My task
in assessing their testimony is affected by their conduct during the marriage,
which has involved some collaborative subterfuge.  During litigation between
Mr. Taylor and the Bank of Nova Scotia, for example, money earned by him was
channelled into a bank account maintained by Mrs. Taylor, in her maiden name,
in order that the Bank not learn of it.  Some of his money also went into bank
accounts in Mrs. Mair's name.   For the same reason, the Candolyn was
registered in the name of Mrs. Mair.

52
As I have said, during the
marriage, Mrs. Taylor's spending money was run through the books of Clive
Taylor Agencies Ltd. as a salary to her.  While some of her allowance might
reflect Mr. Taylor's business interests, the "salary" as a whole
seems difficult to recognize as legitimate.

53
When Mrs. Taylor took her Clive
Taylor Agencies Ltd. 1988 T-4 to Revenue Canada officials, after the
separation, her information was sufficiently interesting to them that a
re-assessment of Clive Taylor Agencies Ltd. was conducted, with negative
consequences for the company.  She went to Revenue Canada because Mr. Taylor
did not plan to come up with the money required for the tax payable on the T-4,
as he had done in past years.

54
I find, that had Mr. Taylor come up
with the money to pay the tax, Mrs. Taylor would not have approached Revenue
Canada.

55
Mr. Taylor, in December 1989, made
significantly misleading representations to his bank as to his net worth and as
to the value of individual assets that he owned.

56
I suppose too much can be made of
this sort of stuff: it does seem fair to say that it makes findings of fact
based on the testimony of these three witnesses more difficult.

57
The long history between Mr. Taylor
and Transamerica presents its own difficulties.  Mr. Taylor is obviously
enormously good at what he does and, hence, a great asset to Transamerica.
From the point of view from Transamerica, the task is to keep Mr. Taylor as a
salesman, with as much incentive as possible to succeed.  Transamerica has
commercial reasons to support what is in Mr. Taylor's interests.

THE ASSETS

58
Rather than using any values given in
evidence, I will confine this analysis to the assets themselves.

(a)
The
Retirement Savings Plans
-- These are family assets, of course.  For the
purposes of division of assets, their value is to be taken as the value as of
the triggering date, plus whatever component of the appreciation since then can
be attributed to the holdings as at the triggering date.

(b)
The
Candolyn
-- The Candolyn is an obvious family asset.  Against what was
realized for it, there may be deducted in the favour of Mr. Taylor the sum of
$7,558.68, representing repair invoices incurred not long after the separation
(of $1,720.39 and $5,838.29.)  The other expenses claimed by Mr. Taylor with
reference to the Candolyn should not diminish the claim of Mrs. Taylor.  They
are attributable to Mr. Taylor's continued and exclusive use of the Candolyn,
even when in the nature of repair.

(c)
The
Jaguar and the motorcycle
-- There was no evidence about the use of the
Jaguar.  With respect to an automobile, I would expect some evidence as the
basis for a submission that an automobile used by one spouse was not used also
from time to time for family purposes.  The Jaguar is a family asset.  The case
of the motorcycle is more clear.  It was used for the family purpose of
enjoying the Candolyn.

(d)
Oxy
Investments Inc.
-- This is not so much a family asset as one in which both
parties were intended to have an interest.  Although I accept the evidence of
Mr. Taylor that Mrs. Taylor never contributed the $5,000.00 which was to
purchase her share, I see this as the least of formalities, in a marriage where
formalities were often at odds with the reality (as in the "ownership"
of the Candolyn by Mrs. Mair).  Mrs. Taylor is entitled to her 1/4 share of
this company, for what it is worth.

(e)
Clive
Taylor Agencies Ltd.
-- This company was the mere alter ego of Mr. Taylor.
The virtue of pursuing an interest in it, before the bankruptcy, had to do with
the prospects of its future income.  That meant that the value of the shares
might depend on actuarial opinions, such as the one given by Transamerica as to
Mr. Taylor's future commission income.  But the existence or non-existence of
Clive Taylor Agencies Ltd., that is, the company itself, would have been
irrelevant to determining whether Mrs. Taylor had an interest in the capital
value of that projected future income; and to give her an interest in the
company now would accomplish nothing.

I
can see no purpose in the exercise.  Clive Taylor Agencies Ltd. is not to be
treated as a family asset.  Alternatively, it should be re-apportioned 100% to
Mr. Taylor.

(f)
Investments
In Shares
--  Nothing in the evidence persuades me that Mrs. Taylor had
anything to do with the buying and selling of shares of stock in limited
companies by Mr. Taylor.  There is no evidence of use of these investments for
a family purpose or that the source of the money used to make the investments
in the first place came from assets used for a family purpose.  These
investments are not family assets.

(g)
MURB
Investments
-- the comments immediately preceding apply.

(h)
The
Insurance Policy on Mrs. Taylor's Life
-- Mr. Taylor is the owner and
beneficiary of a policy of life insurance on the life of Mrs. Taylor, with a
face value of $150,000.00.  He insists that the policy is his to keep.  I am
reluctant to conclude that this is a mere investment on his part: that seems a
little cold-blooded.  The alternative explanation is that the proceeds of the
policy, had Mrs. Taylor died during the marriage, could have helped Mr. Taylor
look after Candice.  On that somewhat tenuous analysis, the policy is a family
asset.  The parties have leave to make submissions as to this finding.

(i)
Richmond
Country Club Membership
-- This membership was in Mr. Taylor's name and
predated the marriage but the privileges of the Club were enjoyed by both.  I
agree with and adopt the analysis of Prowse J. in
McComb v. McComb
[5]
in finding that the
membership is an asset in the hands of Mr. Taylor.  It was also a family asset.

Membership
in such clubs, however, has a notoriously weak market value.

(j)
The
Transamerica "Collateral Estimate"
-- More or less as at the date
of the triggering event, according to the calculations made by Transamerica,
the then present value of future renewal commission income that Mr. Taylor
reasonably could be expected to earn was $320,994.

I
agree with Mr. Taylor that this is not an asset at all, only an estimate.  On
the other hand, it is not a meaningless bookkeeping entry.  It is the informed
opinion of Transamerica.  As such, I would have thought, it was a fairly solid
number.  While realizing on these expectations involves the continuing
commitment of the salesman, that continuing commitment
──
certainly, in the case of Mr. Taylor
──
is to be expected.  The company rated
him at or near the top in "persistency", that is, in maintaining
renewals.  I am sure that Transamerica has a number of reasons why it maintains
this calculation; one of them, I am sure, is to monitor the position of the
agent, with reference to money owed by him to the company.

Despite
its inchoate character, the Collateral Estimate seems to me literally something
that one could take to the bank, in support of, for example, a loan
application.

For
a variety of reasons, Transamerica often makes payments to agents before
commissions have been wholly earned.  In the eyes of the company, money so paid
is a debt owed by the agent to it.  Interestingly, Mr. Taylor did not seem to
think so, at least, so far as disclosing the existence of it to his bankers
went.  I imagine he thought of this item as income in advance, or something
like that.

Again
more or less as at the triggering event, Mr. Taylor's indebtedness to the
company was $326,499, that is, it was virtually in equilibrium with the
Collateral Estimate.  Herbert George Stone, a Divisional Manager for
Transamerica, testified that this was more or less a coincidence and that there
was no necessary relationship between the two figures.  Nonetheless, my
impression is that, ordinarily, Transamerica saw the collateral estimate as its
safety net vis-a-vis the indebtedness.  There may well have been other business
reasons why Transamerica would tolerate indebtedness from an agent, of course.

The
result is that neither the Collateral Estimate or Mr. Taylor's indebtedness to
Transamerica figures in the division of their assets.  However, both need to be
considered in the context of the "Supplementary Plan" maintained by
Mr. Taylor with Transamerica, during the marriage.

(k)
Chattels

-- I agree with Mr. Taylor that some of the personal possessions should be
his.  These are items 1 to 24 and 68 of the Maynard's Appraisal, which appears
at Tab 1 of Exhibit 1.  This is because they came to him from his family and
because some of them have a religious significance for him, as a Jew, which
does not apply to Mrs. Taylor.  I should say, though that, during the marriage,
Mrs. Taylor honoured and observed Jewish traditions, especially with Candice.
Otherwise, although I conclude that Mrs. Taylor took away the majority of the
chattels jointly owned and used by both of them, during the marriage, the
on-the-ground division should not be interfered with.

Although
it is unnecessary for this decision, I record my finding that it was proper for
Mrs. Taylor to remove the chandelier from the family home.  Despite Exhibit 15,
I conclude that her testimony and that of her mother about the chandelier was
truthful.

(l)
The
Transamerica "Supplemental Plan" --
The Supplemental Plan offered
by Transamerica to some of its agents is designed to reward the more successful
among them.

The
company makes contributions to an RSP to which an agent makes contributions, on
a matching basis, but the company's ability to match contributions ceases when
the amount put into the RSP reaches the maximum permitted by law.

The
Supplemental Plan was designed, as its name implies, to augment the RSP
scheme.  Any contributions made to it by an agent are matched by the company.
As at 1984, Mr. Taylor did not have any money invested, either his own or
Transamerica's, in a Supplemental Plan.  By the time of the triggering event in
March 1989, there was $109,200 in the Plan.

One
approach to whether the Supplementary Plan is a family asset is the contention
that, in its true nature, it was a pension.

Some
of the features of the Supplementary Plan constitute an inhibition on
withdrawals.  As well, the evidence of Mr. Taylor was that he could not get
access to the company contributions until he retired.

The
Courts have been prepared to treat as pensions, or at least treat as family
assets, savings plans which have pension characteristics.  For example
in
Rutherford
v. Rutherford
, Seaton J.A., for the Court of Appeal, held as follows:

"I
would read 'a right of a spouse under an annuity or a pension' to include any
right, even one that can be said to be inchoate, contingent, immature, or not
vested.  In short, I would interpret these provisions broadly, so as to give
full effect to the policy adopted by the legislation".
[6]

In
Graff
v. Graff
, Seaton J.A., again for the Court, said:

"Where
assets can be identified as a means of saving to provide a retirement income,
then I think that the considerations apply that would apply to a pension
plan".
[7]

It
is pointed out on behalf of Mr. Taylor that the Supplementary Plan was not a
registered plan for income tax purposes and that his contributions made were in
after-tax dollars.  Participation was voluntary.  Withdrawal of funds was
permitted, even though that carried with it a penalty.  It is also observed
that the Court of Appeal
in
Graff
was dealing with classic,
conventional, registered pension and retirement funds, such as fall
automatically within the meaning of s. 45(3)(d) of the
Family Relations
Act.

But
I think what the Court of Appeal is saying in these decisions is that s.
45(3)(d) has the legislative implication that money set aside during a marriage
for retirement purposes must be taken to have been diverted for a family
purpose.  With that as the starting point, it is not difficult to take the next
step and to recognize that a savings plan which may not fit precisely within
the definition of s. 45(3)(d) may also be impressed with a family purpose.

What
distinguishes the Supplementary Plan in this case from an ordinary investment
is the matching company contribution and the design of the plan, both clearly
oriented to the retirement years.

While
not dispositive of the legal character of the Supplementary Plan, I am
reinforced in identifying it as a "pension" by the letter from
Transamerica to Mr. Taylor of 22nd October 1990 (Exhibit 1, Tab 9), which
identified the Supplementary Plan as part of the total value of Mr. Taylor's
Retirement Savings Plan.  Admittedly, the writer makes the mistake of
characterizing the Supplementary Plan as a registered one; nonetheless, it
identifies the purpose of it.

I
find the Supplementary Plan to be a family asset.

This
makes the submission on the alleged admission in Mr. Taylor's pleadings (that
the Supplementary Plan was a pension) unnecessary to rule upon.

REAPPORTIONMENT

59
I accept the argument put forward on
behalf of the trustee in bankruptcy that it is not open to me to order a
reapportionment of assets which have vested in the trustee, that I am bound by
the holding of Esson J.
in
Biedler v. Biedler
[8]
,
which was followed by Hunter J.
in
Pigeon v. Pigeon
[9]
.

60
A different and attractive result was
reached
in
Thompson v. Thompson
[10]
,
in which Hamilton J. held that the only property of a bankrupt spouse which
vests in his trustee is that to which the bankrupt is entitled under the
combined operation of ss.43 and 51 of the
Family Relations Act
.
However, Hamilton J. confined the ambit of his decision to cases in which a
restraining order over assets had been granted pursuant to s.53 of the
Family
Relations Act
, which is not the case here.  Hamilton J. also recognized
that, otherwise, he was bound to follow
Pigeon
.

61
However, there remains Mrs. Taylor's
interest in assets dealt with by the trustee.  For example, the Candolyn, a
family asset, was sold and the trustee holds the proceeds.  As well, if I
understand the evidence correctly, the trustee declined to bring or attempt to
bring the money held in the Supplementary Plan into the bankruptcy.

62
Since Mr. Taylor is also claiming
reapportionment, he is permitted to argue that he should receive part of the
funds held by the trustee which are earmarked for Mrs. Taylor.  And either
party is entitled to make an argument about reapportionment of assets outside
the bankruptcy.

63
In the main, the evidence about the
assets realized in the bankruptcy which I have held to be family assets
──
the Candolyn, the Jaguar, the
motorcycle
──

does not offer a factual basis for reapportionment.

64
The cases in which an RSP will be
reapportioned must be few and far between.  This is not one of them.

65
The same must be said, it seems to
me, with respect to the Supplementary Plan.  In functional terms, it was a
retirement plan.  The entire value of the Plan by the time of the triggering
event was created when the parties were married and living together.

66
The wrinkle, however, is that
Transamerica applied the money in the Supplemental Fund against Mr. Taylor's
indebtedness to it, after the bankruptcy.  In an affidavit sworn 18th February
1993, Mr. Grieve, counsel for the trustee, described the ability of the trustee
to claim some or all of the Supplementary Plan as a "remaining
issue".  My impression from the affidavit is that, save for a possible
technical oversight on the part of Transamerica, the trustee regarded
TransAmerica as a secured creditor vis-a-vis the Supplementary Plan.

67
In the general welter of assets,
liabilities and trans-actions, the parties must accept the fall-out of the
bankruptcy.  Advantage and disadvantage cross each other.  For example, the
MURBs fall into the maw of the bankruptcy, which benefits both parties.

68
There are special dynamics, though,
which flow from the use made by Transamerica of the Supplementary Plan fund.
Among them is the continuing right of Mr. Taylor to represent the company and
to sell its policies and the terms on which he is allowed to take money out.
It seems reasonable to infer that, to the extent that his indebtedness to the
company has been reduced by diversion of the Supplementary Plan fund, Mr.
Taylor's take-home pay since then has been enhanced.  I understand that he
continues to make payments to reduce his indebtedness to the company; I doubt
that there is anything more to this than the normal balancing of debt versus
projected income.

69
I can see no basis to reapportion
this asset in favour of Mr. Taylor.

CONSEQUENTIAL RELIEF

70
Money is being held by the trustee in
bankruptcy.  Additional money is being held by Mr. Kenneth Glasner, Q.C., on
behalf of Mr. Taylor, representing the proceeds of sale of his home in British
Columbia (after it ceased to be the matrimonial home).

71
My hope is that this judgment will
enable the parties and the trustee to agree as to the distribution of the
assets.  One of the obvious possibilities is that assets held for Mr. Taylor
may have to be diverted to satisfy the entitlement of Mrs. Taylor, as
recognized by this judgment.

72
Failing agreement, the parties may
apply.

"FRASER
J."
